title: A year of weather, two places
interaction: Scrub through one real year of daily weather at a chosen station: each day a bar from the night's low to the afternoon's high and a drop for the rain, the 365 days drawn in a ring. Pick a second place (a desert, a rainy tropical coast, the Arctic, a foggy coast, a snowy interior) and its ring appears beside the first. Flip to the next year: the days are different every time, but the shape of each ring, the climate, comes back.
takeaway: Weather is what happens today and nobody can tell you a month ahead; climate is the shape of the whole year, different in each place and the same from year to year.
needs: Daily high, low and rain for a handful of US stations in contrasting climates (Phoenix for desert, Hilo for wet tropics, Utqiagvik for the Arctic, San Francisco for a coast, Minneapolis for a continental interior) from NOAA GHCN-Daily (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/global-historical-climatology-network-daily); US stations are US Government data, public domain. Non-US stations in GHCN-Daily carry no clear licence, so the page uses US stations only.
needsSource: NOAA GHCN-Daily, US stations only (US Government data, public domain)
pitfall: One cold week does not disprove a warming climate and one hot day does not prove it: the page compares whole years, never single days.
why: NGSS 3-ESS2-1: 'Represent data in tables and graphical displays to describe typical weather conditions expected during a particular season' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/3-ess2-1-earths-systems); England KS1 geography, seasonal and daily weather patterns.
overlapWith: greenhouse-effect (level 1) runs emission scenarios to 2100; this page shows no trend and no model, only measured days, to separate weather from climate before any warming is discussed.

title: Waves at the beach
interaction: A cross-section of sea from deep water to the sand, with a rubber duck floating on it. Watch a wave pass: the duck bobs round in a small circle and ends up where it started, so the water does not travel with the wave. Drag the sea floor to make the beach steeper or gentler: as the water gets shallow the waves slow down, bunch together, grow taller and finally topple and break, far out on a gentle beach and right at the shore on a steep one.
takeaway: A wave carries its shape across the sea while the water only circles in place, and waves break where the water gets too shallow to carry them.
needsSource: none (water waves slowing with depth, growing as they slow, breaking when their height nears the depth; a tracer following the orbital motion)
pitfall: Beach waves are not made by the tide: they are made by wind far out at sea, and the water only rushes forward in the surf, not on the way in.
why: NOAA National Ocean Service, 'Why does the ocean have waves?' (https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/wavesinocean.html); NGSS 4-PS4-1 and England KS3 geography, coasts.
overlapWith: waves-interference (level 1) is a ripple tank of interference, harmonics and Doppler; this page has one wave, a sloping floor and a duck, and sun-earth-moon's tides are not waves.

title: Why clouds form, and why their bottoms are flat
interaction: Drag a bubble of air up from the warm ground: it swells and its thermometer drops about one degree for every hundred metres, which is also why it is colder on a mountain, until the invisible water it carries turns to droplets and the bubble turns white. Every bubble released from the same ground turns white at the same height, so the clouds have flat bottoms; make the day more humid and the cloud base drops, dry the air and clouds form higher or not at all. A last step blows the bubble over a mountain: it rains on the side facing the wind and the air comes down the far side dry.
takeaway: Rising air cools, and a cloud appears at exactly the height where the air gets cold enough for its water to condense, which is why cloud bottoms are flat and why mountains are cold.
needsSource: none (dry-adiabatic cooling of a parcel and the Magnus saturation formula, the standard textbook model)
pitfall: It is not colder on a mountain because it is farther from the Sun: a few kilometres make no difference to sunlight, and the air up there is cold because it has expanded. Clouds are not made of vapour and are not lighter than air: they are droplets falling so slowly that the rising air carries them.
why: UCAR Center for Science Education, 'Clouds and How They Form' (https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/clouds/how-clouds-form); NGSS MS-ESS2-4 on the changes of state in the water cycle.
overlapWith: atmosphere-weather (level 2) shows global convection, pressure systems and fronts; this page follows one bubble of air and one cloud, with no Coriolis and no map.

title: The compass and Earth's magnetic poles
interaction: A globe with a magnet buried inside, its field drawn as lines looping from pole to pole. Drag a compass anywhere on the surface and its needle swings to lie along the local line: near the equator it lies flat along the ground, and near a magnetic pole it tries to point straight down and becomes useless. The magnetic pole sits hundreds of kilometres from the geographic one and drifts year by year, so from most places the needle misses true north by an angle the page measures as you move.
takeaway: A compass does not point at the North Pole: it lines up with Earth's magnetic field, which comes out of a magnetic pole hundreds of kilometres from the geographic one and dips into the ground as you go north.
needs: Earth's field from the World Magnetic Model WMM2025 coefficients, NOAA NCEI (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/world-magnetic-model), US Government work stated as public domain; a tilted offset dipole is the documented fallback.
needsSource: World Magnetic Model WMM2025 coefficients (NOAA NCEI, public domain)
pitfall: The needle is not pulled toward the North Star or the geographic pole, and the magnetic pole is not a fixed place: it has moved hundreds of kilometres in a lifetime.
why: England KS3 physics, Magnetism: 'Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation' and KS2 Year 3 'describe magnets as having 2 poles' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study).
overlapWith: electromagnetism (level 2) covers fields, induction and Maxwell; this page uses one magnet, one needle and a globe, and is the only one where a compass is navigated.

title: Dew, fog and the cold glass
interaction: A glass of iced water stands in a room: drag its temperature down and watch the air touching it, nothing, nothing, then at one particular temperature, the dew point, the glass mists over. Switch to a field at night and drag the night's temperature down: the grass gets wet at the same dew point, keep going and the air itself turns to fog, and if the dew point is below freezing you get frost instead. Make the day more humid and the dew point rises, so the dew comes sooner.
takeaway: Air carries an invisible amount of water, and the moment anything cools it past one particular temperature, the dew point, that water comes out as drops, mist or frost.
needsSource: none (saturation vapour pressure from the Magnus formula, relative humidity, frost point)
pitfall: The water on a cold glass does not leak through the glass: it comes out of the air. Fog is a cloud sitting on the ground, not smoke or steam.
why: England KS2 science, Year 4 States of matter: 'identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study).
overlapWith: states-of-matter (level 1) shows condensation in a box of molecules under temperature and pressure; this page shows it on a glass, on grass and in the air, at one temperature the reader finds by hand.

title: Fossils and rock layers
interaction: Drop a shell, a leaf or a fish onto a sea floor and let mud and sand rain down year after year; add another creature later, and another, and switch the sea for land for a while. The layers pile up, squeeze, harden into rock, and the buried creatures turn to stone. Then cut the cliff: the oldest things lie deepest, and the stretch that was land leaves leaves above shells.
takeaway: Rock layers pile up from the bottom, so in an undisturbed cliff deeper means older, and the fossils in each layer are a snapshot of what lived there then.
needsSource: none (sedimentation and compaction through time, relative dating by superposition; optionally real fossil occurrences from the Paleobiology Database, CC BY 4.0)
pitfall: A fossil is not a bone that survived: it is rock that took the bone's place. And layers are not one per year like tree rings.
why: NGSS 4-ESS1-1: 'Identify evidence from patterns in rock formations and fossils in rock layers to support an explanation for changes in a landscape over time' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/4-ess1-1-earths-place-universe); England KS2 Year 3: 'describe in simple terms how fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock'.
overlapWith: deep-time (level 1) scrubs a dated timeline of 4.5 billion years; this page has no dates at all, only the order of layers and what is buried in them.

title: Heat from underground
interaction: Drill a well down from a field and read the thermometer as it goes: the rock gets warmer with every kilometre, warm enough for a bath a few kilometres down and for steam in volcanic ground. Pump water down and up to heat a town and watch the ground around the well cool over years, then rest it and watch the heat creep back; move the well to Iceland or beside a hot spring and compare. A map shows the heat measured flowing out of the ground around the world.
takeaway: The ground gets hotter the deeper you go, so a deep enough well reaches heat that can warm a house or boil water, soonest where volcanoes are near.
needs: Measured heat flow out of the ground around the world, for the map and the local gradient: the IHFC Global Heat Flow Database (CC BY 4.0).
pitfall: Underground heat is not the Sun's heat stored in the ground: the Sun warms only the top few metres, and below that the warmth comes from the Earth itself. Nor is it endless at one spot: pump too fast and the rock around the well cools for decades.
why: US DOE, 'Geothermal basics', https://www.energy.gov/eere/geothermal/geothermal-basics (curriculum: NGSS 4-ESS3-1, energy resources)
overlapWith: plate-tectonics: that page shows where volcanoes are and why; this page follows the heat down a well anywhere, and what pumping it out does to the ground.
needsSource: IHFC Global Heat Flow Database, https://ihfc-iugg.org/products/global-heat-flow-database (CC BY 4.0).

title: Glaciers: rivers of ice
interaction: A mountain valley in cross-section, with snow falling on the high ground and melting on the low ground; press play and the snow that outlasts the summer packs into ice, and the ice, once thick enough, creeps downhill like very slow honey, dragging rocks that scrape the valley into a U. The one control is the climate: make it colder or snowier and the front advances, warmer and the front retreats. Flags frozen into the ice show that the ice itself still flows forward even while the front is retreating.
takeaway: A glacier is a slow river of ice whose front moves forward or back depending on whether the snow it gains up high outpaces the melting at its toe, while the ice itself always flows downhill.
needsSource: none (a one-dimensional shallow-ice flowline with Glen's flow law and a snowfall-minus-melt balance that depends on height; PhET's legacy Glaciers sim is the reference interaction)
pitfall: A retreating glacier does not flow backward or uphill: it melts at its toe faster than it flows forward.
why: England KS3 geography: 'glaciation, hydrology and coasts' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-geography-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-geography-programmes-of-study); PhET Glaciers (https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/glaciers).
overlapWith: ice-ages (level 2) explains when ice sheets grow from orbital cycles; this page shows how one glacier flows and why its front moves.

title: How caves form
interaction: A block of limestone threaded with hair-thin cracks, and slightly acid rainwater seeping in from the top; press play with the clock running thousands of years. Water flows where it can and dissolves a little rock as it goes, and every crack it widens carries more water and so widens faster, until one path wins and swells into a tunnel while the others stay cracks; the one control is how acid the rain is. Lower the water table and the tunnel drains into an air-filled cave where drips start building stalactites.
takeaway: Caves are dissolved, not dug: the crack that carries the most water widens fastest, so a maze of hair-thin cracks turns into one big tunnel.
needsSource: none (a fracture-network karst model: flow through a crack growing with the cube of its width, dissolution from the standard calcite kinetics, a sped-up clock)
pitfall: Most caves were not washed out by underground rivers or cracked open by earthquakes: the rock was dissolved, slowly, by water that was only slightly acid.
why: England KS3 geography: 'rocks, weathering and soils' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-geography-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-geography-programmes-of-study); US National Park Service, Caves and Karst (https://www.nps.gov/subjects/caves/index.htm).
overlapWith: acids-bases (level 1) shows acids reacting; this page is about a positive feedback in flow, and the acid is only the thing that does the dissolving.

title: From cloud droplet to raindrop, or hailstone
interaction: A cloud of tiny droplets hangs in gently rising air, each falling slower than the air rises, so the cloud floats; press play and droplets bump and merge, and the bigger one gets the faster it falls and the more it sweeps up, until it outruns the updraft and drops out as rain, a size scale showing the drop is a hundred droplets across and took about a million of them. The one control is the updraft: turn it up and the drops grow larger before they fall, the difference between drizzle and a downpour. Turn it up to thunderstorm strength and the drops are carried above the freezing height, where each trip up adds a layer of ice until a hailstone too heavy for the wind drops out, and you can cut it open and count the rings.
takeaway: A cloud droplet must merge with about a million others before it falls faster than the air that holds the cloud up, so rain is the end of a chain of collisions, and the stronger the rising air, the bigger what finally falls, up to hail.
needsSource: none (collision-coalescence growth with terminal velocities from the standard published fall-speed relation for water drops, and an ice sphere's fall speed against the updraft for the hail step)
pitfall: Raindrops are not tear-shaped: small ones are spheres and big ones flatten into buns. A cloud does not rain because it has become too heavy, and hail is not frozen rain and does not need a cold day: it falls from summer thunderstorms whose tops are far below freezing.
why: NGSS MS-ESS2-4, whose clarification stresses 'the ways water changes its state as it moves through the multiple pathways of the hydrologic cycle' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ess2-4-earths-systems); NGSS 3-ESS3-1 on weather-related hazards (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/3-ess3-1-earth-and-human-activity).
overlapWith: cloud-base: that page ends where a cloud appears; this one asks why its droplets stay up and what has to happen before they come down.

title: Lighthouses: how far a light can be seen
interaction: Raise a lighthouse's lamp up its tower and watch the lit stretch of sea grow as the Earth's curve stops hiding it; a ship sails in from beyond the horizon and its lookout sees the flash first from the crow's nest, then from the deck. Spin the lamp's lens to send a beam round and set its rhythm of flashes from a real list of lights; the ship reads the rhythm to tell this lighthouse from the next one down the coast.
takeaway: The Earth's curve hides a low light, so lighthouses are tall and lookouts climb high, and each light's rhythm of flashes is its name.
needs: Heights, ranges and flash characteristics of a few named lighthouses from the US Coast Guard Light List (US government work, public domain).
pitfall: A light is not hidden by distance alone: on a flat Earth a bright enough lamp would be seen from anywhere. The lens does not make the lamp brighter; it gathers light that would be wasted upward and sideways into a beam, which is why the light flashes as the beam sweeps past.
why: The US Coast Guard Light List, the real register of lights and their characteristics, https://www.navcen.uscg.gov/light-lists ('how far can you see a lighthouse' is a common search question)
overlapWith: light-optics: that page traces rays through lenses on a bench; this page does not trace the lens at all, it uses the curve of the Earth and the rhythm of flashes.
needsSource: USCG Light List (public domain), https://www.navcen.uscg.gov/light-lists

title: Lightning and thunder: count the seconds
interaction: A storm scene: a charged cloud, open ground and a palette of things to place on it (a tree, a house, a tall rod, a person); press strike and a branching bolt grows down from the cloud step by step, landing on the tallest thing near its path more often than anywhere else. Then the flash reaches the viewer at once while the thunder's sound front crawls out at a third of a kilometre per second, a counter ticking off the seconds until it arrives. Drag the viewer farther away: more seconds, fainter rumble.
takeaway: Thunder is the sound of the lightning you already saw: light arrives at once and sound takes about three seconds per kilometre, so counting the gap tells how far away the storm is, and the bolt favours the tallest path to the ground.
needsSource: none (the dielectric-breakdown model of Niemeyer, Pietronero and Wiesmann, 1984, grown on a grid with grounded objects; sound at 343 m/s)
pitfall: Thunder is not clouds bumping together, and lightning does strike the same place twice: tall things get hit again and again.
why: US National Weather Service, 'Understanding Lightning: Thunder', with the count-the-seconds rule (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-science-thunder); KS2 Year 4 Sound: 'sounds get fainter as the distance from the sound source increases'.
overlapWith: waves-interference (level 1) treats sound as a wave with speed and Doppler shift; this page uses only the fact that sound is slow and light is not, plus where a bolt goes.

title: How rivers carve valleys
interaction: Rain falls on a bumpy block of land shown from above and in cross-section. Water runs downhill, joins into streams, picks up soil where it runs fast and drops it where it slows: the streams branch like a tree, cut valleys, and a fan of dropped mud grows where the river meets the sea. One control: how much it rains; a later step lifts the land to see the rivers cut faster.
takeaway: Rivers do not just follow valleys, they make them: moving water carries the land downhill a grain at a time and drops it wherever it slows.
needsSource: none (a cellular hydraulic-erosion model: flow routing on a small grid, erosion by fast water with a carrying limit, deposition where it slows, hillslope creep; optionally a real hillside from USGS 3DEP elevation, public domain)
pitfall: A valley is not a crack that opened: the river removed what used to fill it, and it took far longer than a lifetime.
why: NGSS 4-ESS2-1: 'Make observations and/or measurements to provide evidence of the effects of weathering or the rate of erosion by water, ice, wind, or vegetation' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/4-ess2-1-earths-systems); England KS2 geography, rivers.
overlapWith: plate-tectonics (level 1) builds mountains; this page wears them down, and it is the only page where water shapes the land.

title: Where sand comes from
interaction: Step a chunk of rock down a river: it breaks off a cliff, bangs along in a flood, and at each stop it is rounder and smaller as its corners knock off, faster for soft rock than hard. Where the river slows, the grains it carries settle by size, boulders first, then gravel, then sand, with mud going farthest; at the beach the waves finish the job. Scrub back and forth along the river to see where each size ends up.
takeaway: Every grain of sand on a beach is a piece of a mountain that was knocked smaller and rounder on its way down, and the river sorts the grains by size as it slows.
needsSource: none (Sternberg's law of downstream abrasion with published coefficients for a few rock types, and settling speeds by grain size)
pitfall: Sand is not all ground up by the sea, and not all sand is quartz: white tropical sand is broken shell and coral.
why: England KS2 science, Year 3 Rocks: 'compare and group together different kinds of rocks on the basis of their appearance and simple physical properties' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study); NGSS 4-ESS2-1.
overlapWith: river-valleys: that page shows the land being cut; this one follows a single rock through the cutting and asks what becomes of it.

title: How dunes march
interaction: A flat bed of sand under a steady wind, drawn as little stacked slabs; press play and the wind lifts grains from the side facing it and drops them a little downwind, they pile until a slope gets too steep and slides, and out of a flat bed grows a field of dunes, each with a gentle face toward the wind and a steep slip face behind. The one control is the wind's direction, later its strength. Turn the wind and the dunes slowly rebuild to face it; everything creeps downwind.
takeaway: Dunes are the wind moving sand uphill one grain at a time and the sand sliding down the back, so a whole dune walks downwind and always faces into the wind.
needsSource: none (Werner's 1995 cellular dune model: sand slabs, wind shadows, avalanching at the angle of repose)
pitfall: Deserts are not defined by sand or by heat but by dryness: most desert is rock and gravel, and some of it is cold.
why: NGSS 4-ESS2-1, erosion by wind (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/4-ess2-1-earths-systems); US National Park Service, 'Aeolian (Dunes) Landforms' (https://www.nps.gov/subjects/geology/aeolian-landforms.htm).
overlapWith: rock-to-sand makes the grains; this page is what the wind does with them, and no existing page shows a landform built by wind.

title: Where wind comes from: the sea breeze
interaction: A coast in cross-section, land on one side and sea on the other, filled with air drawn as drifting particles. Drag the Sun across the sky: by afternoon the land is warmer than the sea, the air over it rises, and air from the sea slides in underneath as a breeze that a flag on the beach shows. At night the land cools faster than the water and the breeze turns around and blows out to sea.
takeaway: Wind is air moving from where it is cool and heavy toward where it is warm and rising, so uneven heating of land and water is enough to make a wind blow, and to turn it around at night.
needsSource: none (a small 2D buoyant-convection solver on a coarse grid, with the sea slower to warm than the land)
pitfall: Warm air does not rise because heat goes up: it rises because it is lighter than the cooler air around it, which pushes it up.
why: NOAA JetStream, 'The Sea Breeze' (https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/ocean/sea-breeze); NGSS MS-ESS2-5 on air masses moving from high to low pressure.
overlapWith: atmosphere-weather (level 2) heats a whole spinning globe into convection cells and winds with Coriolis; this page heats one beach and gets one wind, no rotation.

title: Why snowflakes have six arms
interaction: Start from a speck in cold, moist air and watch a crystal grow on a honeycomb grid: water molecules arrive from all sides, the corners that stick out catch more of them, and six arms shoot out and branch. One control: the amount of moisture in the air, then the temperature. Low moisture grows flat plates and stubby prisms, high moisture grows branching stars, and a little randomness means no two crystals come out the same, though every one keeps its six-fold symmetry.
takeaway: Six-fold symmetry comes from the way water molecules pack, and the shape of the arms comes from the air the crystal grew in, so every snowflake is a record of its own journey.
needsSource: none (Reiter's 2005 hexagonal cellular automaton for snow crystal growth, or the Gravner-Griffeath 2008 model, checked against the Nakaya morphology diagram)
pitfall: Snowflakes are not frozen raindrops; that is sleet. A snow crystal grows from vapour straight into ice.
why: NOAA, 'How do snowflakes form? Get the science behind snow' (https://www.noaa.gov/stories/how-do-snowflakes-form-science-behind-snow); KS2 Year 4 states of matter.
overlapWith: states-of-matter (level 1) shows water freezing into its open lattice; this page shows a single crystal growing from vapour and why its shape depends on the air.

title: What soil is made of: the jar test
interaction: Scoop soil from a chosen place (a sandy garden, a clay field, a forest floor, a river bank) into a jar of water, shake it and step the clock: after a minute the sand has dropped to the bottom, after an hour the silt lies on top of it, and a day later the cloudy water has finally let its clay down, while bits of rotted leaf and root still float. A ruler reads the thickness of each layer and names the soil from the mix. A last step pours water on each soil: it runs straight through the sandy one and sits for hours on the clay.
takeaway: Soil is rock ground into grains of three sizes plus the rotted remains of living things, and the mix decides whether water runs through it or stays.
needsSource: none (settling speeds by grain size from Stokes' law, the sand, silt and clay size classes and the USDA soil texture triangle, US Department of Agriculture work, public domain)
pitfall: Soil is not dirt that was always there and is not the same everywhere: a few centimetres take centuries to form, and the floating bits are as much a part of soil as the grains.
why: England KS2 science, Year 3 Rocks: 'recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study); the jar test is a standard extension-service activity (https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/soil-texture-analysis-the-jar-test/).
overlapWith: rock-to-sand: that page sorts grains by size along a river; this one sorts them in a jar the reader can shake at home and adds the half of soil that was never rock.

title: How a tornado spins up
interaction: A wide, slowly turning column of air under a thunderstorm, drawn as rings of particles. Drag the storm's updraft to stretch the column taller and thinner: the particles keep their swing but have less room, so they whirl faster, like a skater pulling in her arms, and a funnel appears where the whirl is fast enough for the pressure drop at its heart to make a cloud. Let the column widen again and it slows and the funnel fades.
takeaway: A spinning column of air spins faster when it is stretched thinner, and the funnel you see is just the place where the whirl is fast enough to make a cloud.
needsSource: none (a Rankine-type vortex with angular momentum conserved under stretching, particle advection, and the pressure drop that condenses the funnel)
pitfall: The visible funnel is not the whole tornado: the wind spins just as hard outside it before the cloud appears, which is why damage starts before the funnel seems to touch down.
why: NGSS 3-ESS3-1, weather-related hazards (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/3-ess3-1-earth-and-human-activity); 'how do tornadoes form' is a standing how-does-it-work question.
overlapWith: atmosphere-weather (level 2) grows a hurricane from a warm sea on a rotating globe; this page stretches one small vortex with no Coriolis effect at all.

title: Why some volcanoes explode and others ooze
interaction: Step magma up a pipe toward the surface with gas dissolved in it like a shaken fizzy drink: as the weight of rock above lessens, bubbles appear and grow. The one control is how runny or sticky the magma is: runny magma lets the bubbles float out, and lava fountains and flows spill gently down the slope, while sticky magma traps them until the froth bursts and the cone blows its top in ash. A second control adds more gas and makes the sticky case worse.
takeaway: What makes an eruption explosive is not how hot the magma is but how hard it is for its gas to get out: runny magma fizzes, sticky magma bursts.
needsSource: none (bubble growth as pressure falls, bubble rise speed set by the magma's viscosity, fragmentation above a gas fraction threshold)
pitfall: Lava is not fire and a volcano is not a hole into a burning centre: magma is melted rock, and most of the Earth's inside is solid.
why: USGS FAQ, 'How do volcanoes erupt?', runny magma that lets gas escape against sticky magma that traps it (https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/how-do-volcanoes-erupt); England KS2 geography, volcanoes and earthquakes.
overlapWith: plate-tectonics (level 1) shows where volcanoes are and why; this page shows what happens inside one when it erupts, which that page does not.

title: The water cycle
interaction: A sea, a mountain and the sky, with the water drawn as a few hundred dots that the page follows one by one. Turn the Sun up and more dots leave the sea as invisible vapour, rise, cool and gather into clouds that rain on the mountain, from where streams carry them back to the sea; turn it down and the air dries and the rivers shrink. A counter shows how many dots are in the sea, the air, the ice and the rivers at any moment, and the sea always holds almost all of them.
takeaway: Water is never used up: the same water goes round and round between sea, air and land, lifted by the Sun's heat and brought back down by gravity.
needsSource: none (the share of water in each store from the USGS Water Science School, US Government work, public domain)
pitfall: Evaporation does not need boiling: water leaves the sea at ordinary temperatures, faster when it is warmer. And the vapour is invisible; the white of a cloud is droplets.
why: England KS2 science, Year 4 States of matter: 'identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle' and 'associate the rate of evaporation with temperature' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study); also NGSS MS-ESS2-4 (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ess2-4-earths-systems).
overlapWith: carbon-cycle: the same idea of stores joined by flows, but for water, with every drop followed as a particle in a landscape instead of flows drawn to scale between boxes.

title: Why the sea is salty
interaction: A lake fed by a river that carries a pinch of salt in every bucket of water; the Sun lifts pure water out and the salt stays. Open or close the lake's outlet: with an outlet the salt leaves as fast as it arrives and the lake stays fresh, close it and the salt count climbs year after year until crystals ring the shore, like the Dead Sea. Then the ocean: rivers in, evaporation out, and salt also leaving into the sea floor, so its saltiness holds steady at about two teaspoons of salt in every glass.
takeaway: Rivers carry a little salt to the sea and the Sun takes only the water back, so salt collects wherever water can leave only by evaporating.
needsSource: none (a salt mass-balance box model; seawater at about 35 g per kg and the average river at about 0.1 g per litre, from the USGS Water Science School, US Government work)
pitfall: The ocean is not getting steadily saltier today: salt leaves into the sea floor about as fast as rivers bring it.
why: USGS Water Science School, 'Why is the ocean salty?' (https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/why-ocean-salty); 'why is the sea salty?' is among the questions UK parents say they cannot answer (https://www.stornowaygazette.co.uk/arts-and-culture/top-30-impossible-questions-that-children-ask-840687).
overlapWith: ocean-currents (level 2) uses salinity to drive the deep circulation; this page asks where the salt came from and never mentions currents.
